summary.text: Greenhouse gases are the gases in an atmosphere that absorb heat radiated by a planet's surface, raising its surface temperature.
Without them Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of today's 15 °C.
Since about 1750 human activity has raised carbon dioxide by over 50% and methane by 150%, and CO₂ now drives about three-quarters of global warming.

facts.label: Methane versus CO₂
facts.value: About 84 times stronger per mass over 20 years

items.prompt: Argon makes up 0.9% of the air yet traps no heat, while far scarcer carbon dioxide does. What makes the difference?

options.label: Argon atoms are too heavy to absorb heat
CO₂ mixes its elements, so its charge is uneven
CO₂ is a darker gas that soaks up sunlight
Argon sinks to the ground and never rises

items.explain: Argon is monatomic and transparent to thermal radiation, while CO₂'s atoms of different elements give an uneven charge that lets its vibrations interact with infrared.

items.prompt: Imagine every greenhouse gas vanished from Earth's air while sunlight stayed the same. About what would the average surface temperature be?

options.label: About 15 °C
About 30 °C
About −100 °C
About −18 °C

items.explain: Without greenhouse gases the surface would average about −18 °C rather than the present 15 °C.

items.prompt: Water vapor is the biggest greenhouse gas, yet large irrigation schemes barely change its global level. Why?

options.label: It leaves the air within about nine days
Oceans absorb all the extra vapor at once
It drifts up and escapes into space
Irrigation water never evaporates at all

items.explain: Irrigation can change local water vapor, but its short residence time of about nine days limits any global effect.

items.prompt: A factory releases one burst of methane and one burst of carbon dioxide. Which gas will linger in the atmosphere far longer?

options.label: Methane, by thousands of years
Both leave within a few years
Carbon dioxide, by a long way
Both stay about equally long

items.explain: Methane lasts about 12 years on average, while the carbon cycle takes thousands of years to fully absorb CO₂.

items.prompt: As greenhouse gases build up, the lower atmosphere warms. What happens to the thin upper atmosphere?

options.label: It warms even faster than the surface
It thickens as heat rises into it
It stays the same, as too little gas is there
It cools and shrinks

items.explain: Heat re-emitted in the thin upper layers tends to escape to space, so added greenhouse gases cool the upper atmosphere and make it shrink.

items.prompt: A change means more energy arrives at the top of the atmosphere than leaves it. How is this described, and what follows?

options.label: Positive forcing, leading to warming
Negative forcing, leading to warming
Positive forcing, leading to cooling
Negative forcing, leading to cooling

items.explain: Positive forcing, as from more greenhouse gases, means more energy arriving than leaving, which causes extra warming.

pack.title: Trace Gases, Big Heat
pack.question: How can gases that are a tiny part of the air warm a whole planet?

beats.title: Trace Gases, Big Heat
beats.hook: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide together make up less than 0.1% of Earth's air, yet they still produce a greenhouse effect.

beats.prompt: Sunlight stays the same, but every greenhouse gas is removed from Earth's air. What happens to the average surface temperature?
beats.explain: Sunlight warms the surface, which radiates heat that greenhouse gases mostly absorb; without them Earth would average about −18 °C instead of 15 °C.

choices.label: It rises, as more sunlight gets through
choices.feedback: Greenhouse gases mainly absorb the heat the surface radiates, so removing them lets heat escape rather than adding warmth.

choices.label: It stays near 15 °C
choices.feedback: Sunlight is unchanged, but the heat the surface radiates would no longer be absorbed on its way out.

beats.prompt: Sort each gas by how it handles the heat Earth radiates.
beats.explain: Molecules made of different elements have an uneven charge that lets them interact with infrared radiation, while single-atom argon lets thermal radiation pass.

beats.prompt: Match each gas to what is true of it.

right.label: Lasts about 12 years in the air
Stays in the air about nine days
Causes about three-quarters of global warming

beats.explain: Each gas differs in how long it stays in the air and how much warming it drives.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the recent rise of greenhouse gases in order.

items.label: CO₂ has climbed its first 30 ppm
CO₂ has climbed a further 90 ppm

beats.explain: The first 30 ppm rise ran from the Industrial Revolution around 1750 to 1958, the next 90 ppm came by 2014, and warming hit 0.27 °C per decade over 2015–2024.

beats.idea: Gases whose molecules can interact with infrared radiation absorb the heat Earth's surface gives off, so even small amounts change how warm the planet is.

paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Greenhouse gases are the gases in an atmosphere that trap heat and so raise the surface temperature of a body such as Earth. Sunlight warms Earth's surface, the surface gives off heat, and greenhouse gases soak up most of that heat; this is the greenhouse effect. Without them, Earth's surface would average about −18 °C (0 °F) instead of today's 15 °C (59 °F).

paragraphs.heading: Why only some gases
paragraphs.text: What sets these gases apart is that they are infrared active: they absorb and give off infrared radiation in the same long wavelengths that Earth's surface, clouds and air emit. Argon, 0.9% of the air, is made of single atoms and lets heat radiation pass straight through. Carbon dioxide (0.04%), methane, nitrous oxide and rarer trace gases add up to less than 0.1% of the atmosphere. But their molecules join atoms of different elements, which makes their electric charge lopsided and lets their vibrations interact with radiation, and that is why they cause a greenhouse effect.

paragraphs.heading: The energy balance
paragraphs.text: Earth absorbs part of the Sun's energy and sends the rest back to space as reflected light or as heat. A planet's surface temperature depends on the balance between energy coming in and energy going out, and when that balance shifts, the surface warms or cools. Such a shift is measured as radiative forcing, in watts per square meter. More greenhouse gas is a positive forcing: more energy arrives than leaves at the top of the atmosphere, so the planet warms.

paragraphs.heading: Water vapor
paragraphs.text: Water vapor is the most important greenhouse gas overall, causing 41–67% of the greenhouse effect. Yet human activity does not directly change how much there is worldwide; irrigation can affect it locally, but vapor stays in the air only about nine days. Instead it responds to the other gases: warmer air holds more water vapor per unit volume, by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, which adds more warming. This is called water vapor feedback.

paragraphs.heading: What humans have added
paragraphs.text: Since the Industrial Revolution began around 1750, human activity has raised carbon dioxide by over 50% and methane by 150%. Carbon dioxide causes about three-quarters of global warming, and methane most of the rest. Most human CO₂ comes from burning fossil fuels, with agriculture and industry adding the remainder, while methane comes from agriculture, fossil fuel production, waste and other sources. The two linger very differently: methane lasts about 12 years on average, but the carbon cycle needs thousands of years to fully take CO₂ back out of the air.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the rise
paragraphs.text: The amount of a greenhouse gas is usually stated by volume, as parts per million (ppm) or as parts per billion (ppb). A CO₂ level of 420 ppm means 420 of every million air molecules are CO₂. The first 30 ppm of increase took about 200 years, from the Industrial Revolution to 1958, while the next 90 ppm came in just 56 years, up to 2014. Carbon dioxide levels are now higher than at any time in three million years.

paragraphs.heading: Where this is heading
paragraphs.text: Human-caused warming is now rising faster than at any time since measurements began, reaching 0.27±0.1 °C each decade during 2015–2024. If emissions keep going at today's rates, warming will go beyond 2.0 °C (3.6 °F) at some point from 2040 to 2070. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) calls that level dangerous.
